final.title: Tool consolidation is a design constraint, not a rebuild
final.body:
If you run a small business, tool consolidation is not mainly a software question. Treat it as a design constraint: keep the tools you already use, and add one thin automation layer only where a handoff is repeated, rule-based, and worth the extra moving part. Replacing every app usually creates more switching cost than it removes.

A practical test is simple. List the tools in one recurring workflow, then trace the manual handoffs between them: CRM, email, invoicing, documents, calendar, and so on. Pick the step that causes the most delay or error. If that handoff repeats weekly, touches two or more tools, and has a clear outcome, it is a candidate for a bounded workflow. If it is one-off, low-frequency, or outside Bareni’s current scope discipline, the manual route may still be the cheaper choice.

That scope discipline includes high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work, bulk cold-email automation, and scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows. Money movement and other high-risk decisions stay human-approved.

The point is not to force a rebuild. It is to map one recurring handoff, then ask whether consolidation reduces friction or just rearranges it. If it only rearranges it, leave the stack alone.
